atlas-nl.0135: International employers recruit from abroad in English; for most others, a Dutch degree and a local network come first.
atlas-nl.0136: Some programmes close the door to those without existing work rights or a Dutch degree: Heineken’s asks for work rights and Booking.com’s graduate programmes are open only to graduates of Dutch universities.
atlas-nl.0137: 7.8% of ads say Dutch is not needed, the highest share Indeed found, but graduate roles in client-facing work still ask for Dutch.
atlas-nl.0138: ING asks for the application in English and fluent English, while Heineken’s programme asks for both Dutch and English.
atlas-nl.0139: Programmes run in steps: ING takes a CV, motivational questions and grade lists, then HR interviews and business panels at its Amsterdam headquarters (18 to 22 May and 1 to 5 June 2026 for the October class), with a second round only if places remain; a failed assessment or interview cannot be retried.
atlas-nl.0140: Heineken asks for a CV and cover letter, then an online assessment of situational scenarios and a cognitive test, then an introductory call; Unilever runs an online application, a digital assessment of motivation, personality and cognitive ability, a digital interview, and an in-person Discovery Centre in Rotterdam where you learn the outcome the same day.
atlas-nl.0141: Ordinary interviews are conversational, last 30 to 90 minutes, and second and even third rounds are common; you may get a job-related test or tasks. Dress smartly, arrive early, expect direct questions and value modesty over bragging.
atlas-nl.0142: Interviews are normally in English for international employers and in Dutch for Dutch-speaking ones; no source read gives a typical time from application to offer outside the programme calendars.
atlas-nl.0143: A probation period must be agreed in writing and be equal for both sides: none in a contract of six months or less, at most one month in a contract of more than six months and under two years, and at most two months otherwise.
atlas-nl.0144: Holiday allowance is at least 8% of gross annual salary, normally paid in May or June; the default notice period for the employee is one month. Pay scales set by collective agreements cannot be negotiated.
atlas-nl.0145: Successive fixed-term contracts become permanent after three contracts or 36 months, whichever comes first, and a gap of more than six months breaks the chain; a law adopted in July 2026 extends that gap to three years from 1 January 2028.
atlas-nl.0146: After you accept an offer there is a short conversation about employment terms; before accepting, check the contract for trial period, hours, salary, holiday pay and the collective agreement. The pages read do not say how long you have to decide.
atlas-nl.0147: The employer must be a sponsor recognised by the IND, listed in a public register updated once a month, and the IND must decide within 90 days; the employer applies and pays the €423 fee. Ask early whether a prospective employer is on the register.
atlas-nl.0148: For 2026 the gross monthly salary floors are €4,357 for under-30s, €5,942 for 30 and over and €3,122 for those within three years of graduating or on the orientation-year permit; fixed allowances count, holiday allowance does not.
atlas-nl.0149: Some graduate programmes ask for existing work rights and offer no visa support: Heineken’s Netherlands programme asks for Dutch, English and the right to work, and Booking.com’s graduate programmes are for Dutch-university graduates.
atlas-nl.0150: Central government: Werken voor Nederland, filterable by field and education level, with traineeships, internships and starter positions.
atlas-nl.0151: Graduate programmes and events: employers’ own pages (ING, ABN AMRO, Heineken, Unilever, FrieslandCampina) and Magnet.me, which lists employer events such as McKinsey’s Future Talent Program and Strategy&’s Own Your Impact.
atlas-nl.0152: Fairs: De Nationale Carrièrebeurs (RAI Amsterdam), Career Expo Eindhoven at TU/e and Delft Career Days; Career Compass Netherlands, on 28 May 2026 at Eindhoven, was aimed at international students and graduates.
atlas-nl.0153: Permits: the IND’s register of recognised sponsors shows which employers can hire from abroad; the UWV (via werk.nl) supports jobseekers on benefit.
atlas-nl.0154: Missing the window: Heineken’s Netherlands tracks were open for about three weeks, and Unilever fills first come, first served and requires you to finish the digital interview before the period ends.
atlas-nl.0155: Assuming English is enough: the 7.8% of ads that say Dutch is not needed is the highest in Europe, but still means about nine in ten want Dutch in some measure.
atlas-nl.0156: Raising salary in the first interview, bragging, or taking direct questions personally: Dutch interviewers value honesty and modesty.
atlas-nl.0157: Putting a photo, date of birth or marital status on the CV out of habit, or sending a letter longer than one page.
atlas-nl.0158: Applying twice to ING after failing its assessment or interview: the posting says you cannot apply again.
atlas-nl.0159: ING asks for its application in English and fluent English; no Dutch requirement is named for the traineeships read, and no certificate: the motivational questions and interviews are the evidence.
atlas-nl.0160: Heineken’s Netherlands Global Graduate Program asks for Dutch and English; no certificate is named, and the level is judged in the interviews.
atlas-nl.0161: Only 7.8% of Dutch ads say Dutch is not needed, so English-only technology roles are the exception outside the large employers; Booking.com’s programmes require a Dutch-university degree.
atlas-nl.0162: RSM reports that 95.8% of its master’s graduates were employed within six months (512 responses from 2,055 graduates, surveyed in April 2026), and of the 381 who gave timing, 52% had a job before they graduated; this is a school-reported figure with a 25% response rate.
atlas-nl.0163: For internationals the picture is slower: 25% are still in the Netherlands five years after graduating, and of those who stay, 80% are employed at year five.
atlas-nl.0164: The vacancy rate fell from 4.1% in the last quarter of 2024 to 3.9% in the last quarter of 2025, with 5.0% in professional, scientific and technical activities.
atlas-nl.0165: No source read gives a return-offer rate for Dutch graduation internships or a time to first job for internationals.
atlas-nl.0166: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa, work permit or residence document; the immigration service (IND) can confirm your right of residence for €85 if you want proof.
atlas-nl.0167: Staying more than four months, register with the municipality within five days of arriving and you get your citizen service number (BSN) on the spot; for shorter stays there is the non-resident register (RNI).
atlas-nl.0168: A student who works, even one hour a week, must take out Dutch basic health insurance within four months; one who does not work stays on the European Health Insurance Card.
atlas-nl.0170: You cannot apply yourself: your university, a recognised sponsor, applies to the IND. US, UK and some other nationals need no entry visa (MVV).
atlas-nl.0171: Earn at least half of each year’s credits, or the university must report you and the permit is withdrawn.
atlas-nl.0172: Employed work: 16 hours a week in term, or full time in June, July and August, never both, and only once the employer has a work permit (TWV). Freelance work needs no TWV.
atlas-nl.0173: A non-EU student with a student permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days without a Dutch permit, after the university notifies the IND.
atlas-nl.0174: €1,130.77 a month (€13,569.24 a year), plus tuition
atlas-nl.0176: A student who works without Dutch basic health insurance can be fined €529.74 by the CAK, and again.
atlas-nl.0178: An internship your Dutch degree requires needs no work permit, only the Nuffic standard internship agreement signed by you, your university and the company.
atlas-nl.0179: Students of foreign universities and graduates cannot use the Nuffic agreement: the host needs a work permit (TWV) for up to 90 days, or a single permit from the IND for longer, with a real training plan.
atlas-nl.0182: Within three years of a Dutch bachelor’s, master’s or PhD, or of a master’s or PhD from a university in the top 200 of two of THE, QS and ARWU: one year, not renewable, to work in any job without a work permit.
atlas-nl.0183: A job with a recognised sponsor then needs only the lower highly-skilled salary, and keeps it on later renewals and job changes.
atlas-nl.0186: The three years run from the official graduation date on your certificate, not from the ceremony.
atlas-nl.0188: The employer must be a recognised sponsor of the IND; there is no labour-market test, and the IND decides in about two weeks.
atlas-nl.0193: Salary, within three years of a Dutch or top-200 degree
atlas-nl.0194: Any employer established in the Netherlands can hire you, recognised sponsor or not: a contract of at least six months and a three-year degree, or three years of comparable experience in the last seven.
atlas-nl.0195: Salary, graduates of the last three years
atlas-nl.0198: For other jobs the employer applies, after reporting the vacancy to the employment agency UWV at least five weeks ahead and showing no Dutch or EU candidate was found.
atlas-nl.0199: €2,337 gross a month, without holiday pay
